title: Rapid male benefit adaptation in response to sex-limitation, mates, and genetic context in Drosophila melanogaster
content:
Abstract
Intralocus sexual conflict (IaSC) arises when selection favors different trait values in sexes sharing a genetic architecture. Sex-limited selection should allow one sex to adapt without constraint from selection on the other, with intersexual genetic correlations predicted to reduce opposite-sex fitness. In a recent study, male-limited (ML) selection produced the predicted decline in female fitness, but male fitness improvement depended on genetic background, suggesting unintended sources of adaptation. Here, we dissect these responses using a fully factorial assay spanning control- and selection-like conditions, while accounting for the unusual genetic features of the clone-generator (CG) breeding system and specialized CG females used to enforce ML inheritance. We establish substantial but context-dependent improvements in male fitness. Despite this context dependence, we show that phenotypic responses were remarkably consistent: selected males showed enhanced precopulatory traits, including higher mating success and shorter mating latency, while postcopulatory traits, including sperm offense and mate-induced fecundity, remained unchanged. Intriguingly, evolved males also caused substantially less harm to CG females. Together, these findings provide clearer evidence for IaSC, expressed as male-benefit/female-detriment adaptations, while demonstrating that their magnitude and expression were also shaped by the genetic manipulations and mating context of the experimental design.
